questions.text:
A report from a mental health organisation states: 'A survey of 900 randomly selected New Zealand adults found that 38% reported experiencing workplace anxiety in the past year, with a margin of error of 3.3%.'

(i) Calculate the approximate 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all NZ adults who experienced workplace anxiety.
(ii) Verify the margin of error using the rule-of-thumb formula 1/√n.
questions.markingGuide:
Step 1: Achievement: (i) 95% CI ≈ 38% ± 3.3% = (34.7%, 41.3%).

Step 2: (ii) The rule of thumb gives 1/√900 = 1/30 ≈ 0.0333 = 3.3%, which matches the reported margin of error.

Step 3: (A more exact calculation using 1.96·√(p(1 – p)/n) = 1.96 × √(0.38 × 0.62/900) ≈ 1.96 × 0.01618 ≈ 0.0317 ≈ 3.2% is also close.).

questions.text:
The report continues: 'Compared to a 2020 survey using the same methodology, which found 30% of adults experienced workplace anxiety (margin of error 5%, n = 400), there has been a significant increase in workplace anxiety rates.'

Evaluate whether the claim of a significant increase is supported by the data. Show your reasoning.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Merit:
- 2020 CI ≈ 30% ± 5% = (25%, 35%).
- 2025 CI ≈ 38% ± 3.3% = (34.7%, 41.3%).
- The two intervals barely overlap (from 34.7% to 35%) — essentially no overlap, which gives clear evidence of a significant increase from 2020 to 2025.
- The observed difference is 38% – 30% = 8 percentage points.

For Excellence:
- Discusses that (almost) non-overlapping CIs provide strong evidence, notes the same methodology was used (good for comparison), but that changes in how people interpret or report workplace anxiety over 5 years could also contribute to the observed difference.

questions.text:
A study investigated the relationship between screen time and physical activity levels. Researchers collected data from 2,500 university students using an online questionnaire. They found that students who reported more than 4 hours of screen time per day had significantly lower levels of physical activity than those who reported less than 30 minutes.

The researchers concluded: 'Excessive screen time damages physical activity.'

Identify and explain THREE limitations of this study that affect the validity of the conclusion.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Merit:
- (1) Observational study — cannot establish causation.
- People who are already less physically active may turn to screens as a passive alternative (reverse causation).
- (2) Self-reported data — students may inaccurately recall their screen time or physical activity, or under-report (recall bias, social desirability bias).
- (3) Online questionnaire — non-response bias: heavier screen users may be more likely to complete online surveys, skewing the sample.
- (4) Confounding variables — factors such as socio-economic status, study workload, part-time work, health conditions or access to exercise facilities could affect both screen time and activity levels.
- (5) Sample limited to university students — does not generalise to the wider population.
- (6) 'Screen time' is broad — passive scrolling may differ from active use or study-related screen use.

For Excellence:
- At least 3 limitations, each clearly explained with how it specifically undermines the causal claim.

questions.text: Describe how the researchers could redesign this study to better support a causal claim about screen time and physical activity.
questions.markingGuide:
Excellence: A randomised controlled experiment where participants are randomly assigned to different social media limits.

Use objective measures (screen time tracking apps, sleep monitoring devices) rather than self-report.

Control for confounding variables by ensuring groups are similar.

Use a longitudinal design over at least several weeks.

Consider ethical implications — restricting screen time raises questions.

A well-designed observational study with statistical controls for confounders would be more practical.

questions.text:
A regional council report states: 'Our survey of 300 ratepayers found that 72% support the proposed rates increase for roading improvements, with a margin of error of 5.8%. This strong mandate means the council should proceed with the project.'

A ratepayers' group opposes the increase and argues that the survey is misleading because:
• It was mailed only to property owners, not renters
• The response rate was 25% (300 out of 1,200 surveys mailed)
• The survey asked leading questions about road safety

Write a comprehensive evaluation of the survey and the council's claim. In your answer, discuss:
• the sampling method and its limitations
• the margin of error and whether it is valid
• whether the claim of a 'strong mandate' is justified
• what improvements could be made.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Identifies that the low response rate is a problem.

For Merit:
- Explains that the margin of error assumes random sampling, the 25% response rate introduces non-response bias, and property owners may have different views from renters.

For Excellence:
- Comprehensive evaluation covering: (1) Coverage bias — excluding renters, who also pay rates indirectly through rent.
- (2) Non-response bias — only 25% responded, and those who responded may have different views from those who didn't (people who support the rates increase may be more motivated to respond).
- (3) The margin of error is not strictly valid because the formula assumes random responses from the sample, but the 75% non-response rate means the 300 respondents are not representative.
- (4) Leading questions about road safety could push respondents toward supporting the increase.
- (5) The claim of a 'strong mandate' is not justified.
- Improvements: boost response rate through follow-up, include renters, use neutral question wording, use stratified sampling to cover different property types and neighbourhoods.
